System Design & Software Architecture Explained: recursion call stack + memoization (fib(6)) 🔥
How high-performance systems & modern AI operate under the hood!

• Recursion: a function calls itself until the base case
• Call stack: each call pushes a frame (where to return + local state)
• fib(6) live trace: watch frames expand/contract step-by-step
• Exponential re-computation happens fast (why it’s slow)
• Memoization: cache results so repeated calls become O(1) hits

Practical takeaway: In interviews, always ask “what repeats?”—then cache or restructure to cut repeated work.

Debate: Should production code prefer memoization or an iterative DP loop for reliability under load?

Recursion isn’t just a coding pattern—it’s an execution model. In VIZ 22 we live-trace fib(6) to visualize how the recursion call stack grows/shrinks frame-by-frame, then we add memoization to show the “under the hood” performance shift.

What’s happening architecturally:
• Call stack dynamics: each recursive call allocates a frame (return address + locals). Deep recursion risks stack overflow and adds overhead per frame.
• Redundant work in naive Fibonacci: overlapping subproblems recompute the same values repeatedly—classic exponential blow-up.
• Memoization as a caching layer: we trade memory for compute by storing computed results (a targeted form of dynamic programming).

Production trade-offs to consider:
• Memoization memory bounds: unbounded caches can hurt latency and GC/heap stability; use size limits/TTL when appropriate.
• Iterative vs recursive: iterative DP avoids deep stacks and can be more predictable in real services.
• Concurrency: shared caches need careful synchronization or lock-free design; per-request caches are often safer.

Interview lens: When you see recursion, immediately check for overlapping subproblems. If yes, memoization/DP usually wins.
